summary: The video provides a landscape-photography–oriented primer on how meteorology works in three dimensions, with emphasis on terrain–weather interactions (orographics), upper- and lower-atmosphere moisture and cloud formation, and how to leverage live and model data for planning sunrises, sunsets, and dramatic light. The presenter explains why eastern sides of mountain ranges often yield better atmospheric and light conditions for photography, discusses the jet stream and forecast reasoning, and then dives into the practical use of major weather models (ECMWF/EC, GFS, NAM, ICON), ensemble forecasting, and the value of model agreement. Real-time tools covered include PM2.5/dust indicators, swells, webcams, meteograms, and satellite imagery (visible vs infrared) within the Windy app, plus the importance of terrain overlays and terrain-aware forecasts. The discussion culminates in guidance on interpreting National Weather Service forecast discussions as a complementary source to model outputs, and in recognizing the limits of forecasts beyond 48 hours for precise cloud and light conditions.

sections.title: Intro: 3D meteorology and the role of orographics
sections.description: Opening notes establish that meteorology is three-dimensional, with emphasis on how weather systems interact with terrain (orographic effects) and why this matters for landscape photography.

sections.title: Terrain effects on clouds and light; eastern mountain slopes
sections.description: Discussion of how air is forced to rise over mountains, why eastern sides often yield better clouds and light, and how this influences sunrise/sunset opportunities in photography.

sections.title: Jet stream and upper-level winds; forecasting approach
sections.description: Introduction to high-altitude wind patterns, how jet streams steer weather systems, and the general approach forecasters use to predict movement.

sections.title: Weather models and ensemble forecasting
sections.description: Overview of major global models, the origin of ensemble forecasting, and the value of using multiple models to assess forecast confidence through agreement.

sections.title: Model data depth and air-quality dimensions
sections.description: Details on model-derived data layers such as particulate matter and dust, illustrating how air quality can influence visibility and planning.

sections.title: Cloud levels and sunrise/sunset forecasting
sections.description: Guidance on how cloud altitude affects potential sunrises and sunsets, plus practical notes on cloud types to watch for when planning shots.

sections.title: Forecast horizon and reliability; elevation matters
sections.description: Discussion of forecast reliability over different horizons and how targeting specific elevations can change forecast outcomes and photography plans.

sections.title: Point forecasts and meteograms
sections.description: Demonstrates how dropping a pin yields localized forecasts and how meteograms depict cloud evolution and timing for planning.

sections.title: Webcams and satellite tools for real-time planning
sections.description: Explains the use of live webcams and high-definition satellite imagery (visible/infrared) and how looping imagery helps anticipate cloud evolution for optimal light.

sections.title: Terrain overlays, overlays, and real-time interpretation
sections.description: Describes terrain overlays and how topography informs forecast interpretation; discusses the usefulness of overlays and the need to understand geography for accurate forecasting.

sections.title: Forecast discussions and practical interpretation
sections.description: Highlights the value of NWS forecast discussions as expert interpretation of model runs, with guidance on how to decode terminology and gauge forecast certainty.
